chapters.title: How to make a noise
chapters.intro: By the end of this chapter, you will have built a machine that translates electricity into sound.
chapters.payoff:
You may have noticed a pattern:
- A pitch is voltage (`2V` for middle C, `+/- 1V` per octave)
- A control signal (`cv`) is voltage
- The audio signal sent to the **Output** module is voltage

So you may be wondering, *What if I mix and match? What happens if I use an oscillator signal as a control voltage? What about as a pitch signal?*

If so, you're exactly the kind of pervert who is going to really enjoy analog synthesis.
chapters.challenge:
Find out what happens![^1]


[^1]: Hint: add another oscillator module and use it in a dastardly manner.

steps.title: The patch
steps.text:
A *patch* is a catch-all term for any configuration of interconnected synth modules. The term comes from the *patch cables* we use to connect analog synth modules.[^1]

[Click `New patch` in the PATCH panel.](req:new-patch)

[^1]: Long ago, patch cables were used to hot-swap spare equipment into vital communications systems in which something had melted, burned out, or exploded.

    These days, patch cables are mostly used by recreational drug users, commodity fetishists, and the neurodivergent in order to make things go *wubwubwubwub*

steps.title: Add an Oscillator
steps.text:
**Main** here is what is going to send the information from our keyboard circulating through our patch.

Its two most important functions are to send `pitch` (i.e., what note is being played) and `gate`, which answers yes or no to the question, "Is a key being held down right now?"[^1]

The output of **Output** is what you hear. It's can be thought of as the rectum of a patch. A synth patch poops sound into the toilet of the ear.

[Add an **Oscillator** module with `+ Module` in the PATCH panel or the command palette (`Ctrl/Cmd+K` or the `/` key).](req:add-osc)

Any module on the canvas can be moved around by clicking on its header and dragging it around.

[^1]: The caveats, exceptions, and backpedaling that go here are on our feature roadmap and are slated to be added in Q3 of FY 2029

steps.title: Oscillators
steps.text:
An *oscillator* is a machine named after what it does. It oscillates.[^1]

Want it to stop oscillating? Too bad. If it stopped, that would constitute behavior that synth experts call `not oscillating`. For that you would need a completely different kind of machine.[^2]

[Connect **main**’s `pitch` output to the **Oscillator’s** `pitch` input with a patch cable (click one jack and drag to the other jack).](req:main-pitch-osc-pitch)

[Cable **Oscillator** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:osc-out-output-l)

Congratulations! Your machine makes noise.  This noise is continuous.

[^1]: *Oscillation* is any continuous fluctuation over time that is centered around some central value. Synth oscillators emit continuously fluctuating voltage -- traditionally anywhere from 5V to -5V, centered around 0V.

[^2]: These machines are pricey, because they have only ever been made by one company. That company is called Teenage Engineering

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator
steps.text:
Press some keys on the home row of your computer keyboard. You should hear your noise change pitch.

You can do this for a while, but eventually your ears and brain will start to hurt.

When you've had enough, [click on the patch cable between **Oscillator**'s `out` jack and **Output**'s `in` jack to remove the cable.](req:unplug-osc-out-output-l)

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator (cont'd)
steps.text:
Obviously, it would be impractical to unplug your oscillator every time you want a note to stop sounding. Luckily, there is a solution: the *voltage-controlled amplifier (VCA)*.

[Add a **VCA** module.](req:add-vca)

A **VCA** has two important inputs: `in`, for an audio signal, and `cv`, for control voltage. Its `output` is just those two signals multiplied together.

In the next step, we're going to use a **VCA** to multiply **Oscillator**'s  output voltage by zero. This is how we shut up an oscillator.

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator (cont'd) (cont'd)
steps.text:
Let's put the **VCA** to work.

1. [Drag the **Oscillator**’s `out` jack to the **VCA**’s `in` jack.](req:osc-out-vca-in)

2. [Drag the **VCA**’s `out` jack to **Output**’s `l` jack.](req:vca-out-output-l)

Silence. The **Oscillator** is still oscillating, but the **VCA** is closed: nothing is plugged into its `control voltage` jack.

3.  [Drag **main**'s `gate` jack to **VCA**'s `cv` jack.](req:main-gate-vca-cv)

## 4. Press a key on your keyboard's home row. Play a little ditty.

This little machine is starting to resemble an instrument.

steps.title: Gates
steps.text:
Whenever you press a key, here's what's happening:

- The sustained electrical voltage coming through **Main**'s  `pitch` jack changes to represent the pressed key's pitch. `2V` means middle C (aka `C4`). Each volt up or down from there represents an octave. [^1]
- **Main**'s `gate` output voltage, which rests at `0V`, suddenly spikes to `5V`.
- The output signal of **VCA**, which is using **Main**'s `gate` signal as its *control voltage* signal multiplier, suddenly spikes from `0V` to the oscillator's signal voltage multiplied by 5.

[^1]: So the note one octave up from `C4` (aka `C5`) is represented as `3V`.  One semitone up from that (aka `C#5`) is represented as `3.083V`. Why `.083`? Because there are 12 notes in an octave, and `1V/12 = 0.083̅V`.

steps.title: Seeing sound
steps.text:
[Add a **Scope**](req:add-scope) and [cable the **Oscillator**’s `out` into its `a` input](req:osc-out-scope-a).

The screen on the Scope card is what's called an *oscilloscope*.

What you see there is a live visualization of the oscillator's output voltage over time.  You may recognize this squiggle from high school math class as a *wave*.

Conveniently, sound can also be represented as a wave.

*Analog audio* gets its name from the strategy of using changes in voltage as an *analogy* for changes in air pressure.

steps.title: Change the wave
steps.text:
The shape of a wave determines its *timbre*.

Right now, our oscillator emits a `sine` wave -- reminscent of a french horn.  But there are a few other types of wave it can emit. [Hold a note and move its `wave` slider around to hear what they sound like](req:notes).

chapters.title: Shaping sound with envelopes
chapters.intro:
A `gate`, as we learned, is not very subtle. It's either on or off.[^1]

[^1]: (emitting either `0V` or `5V`)

Most real sounds -- a car revving its engine, a car whooshing past you, a mosquito buzzing in your ear, a slap in the ear, a fork hitting a glass of champagne, a drunk person crying -- have shape.

*Shape*, in this context, means a path, traced over time, that starts and ends with a resting value for a certain characteristic, primarily volume, pitch, and timbre.

In sound synthesis, we give sounds this kind of shape using something called an *envelope*.
chapters.payoff: One oscillator now speaks with two different shapes: a swelling pad and a pluck.
chapters.challenge: Make a tiny bell or a very slow sunrise; save both variations.

steps.title: Add an envelope
steps.text:
There are many kinds of envelope. The most common, and the one we're going to use, is an *ADSR* envelope, which is named after its four parameters. An envelope module can control any other module's parameter[^1], but let's consider an example envelope that controls amplitude (volume):
- *attack*: The time that elapses between silence and the sound's peak volume
- *decay*: The time that elapses between peak volume and...
- ... *sustain*: The volume that the signal settles at if the note persists longer than `(attack + decay)` milliseconds.
- *release*: The time that elapses between the end of the note and silence.

[^1]: Including another envelope module's parameters! If there's one thing you should take away from this tutorials is that if it's a parameter, it can be manipulated by control voltage.

    The possibilities are quite literally endless. A synth like the one Wendy Carlos (in-)famously used to record *Switched-On Bach* had something like 10¹³⁴ possible patch cable configurations. Most of them would have sounded like shit, but still.

[Add an **ADSR** module.](req:add-adsr)

steps.title: Controlling note volume with an envelope
steps.text:
Instead of controlling the **VCA** with a simple on/off `gate`, let's give a note's volume some shape.

## First, play a few notes to get a sense of what our starting point sounds like.

[Then click the cable from **Main**’s `gate` to the **VCA**'s `cv` to remove it.](req:unplug-main-gate-vca-cv)

[Connect **Main**'s `gate` to **ADSR**'s `gate`.](req:main-gate-adsr-gate)

Now, instead of controlling note volume directly with `gate` we're using `gate` to control the envelope, which controls the volume: When voltage enters the envelope module through `gate`, volume will
1. increase and peak (`attack`),
2. fade until it reaches its a specific volume ('decay'),
3. remain at that specific volume (aka the 'sustain' volume)  until the gate voltage stops, at which point
4.  volume fades to silence ('release')



[Connect **ADSR**'s `env`(elope) to  **VCA** `cv`](req:adsr-env-vca-cv)

steps.title: Draw the shape
steps.text: [Drag the **ADSR**’s `a` (attack) to about 0.3 s](req:adsr-a) and [`r` (release) to about 1 s](req:adsr-r). Hold a note: it swells in and fades out after you let go.
steps.why: Attack and release are times, sustain is a level. Pads have long attacks and releases; the next step makes the opposite.

steps.title: Make it percussive
steps.text: [Set `a` (attack) to 0.005 s](req:adsr-a), [`s` (sustain) to 0](req:adsr-s) and [`d` (decay) to about 0.2 s](req:adsr-d). Hold a note: it rings out and dies although the key is still down. Plucked and struck sounds have no sustain.

steps.title: A pluck or a pad?
steps.text: Play a few short notes on the keys and hear the pluck die before the next one. Optional: compare `attack` 0.3 s, `sustain` 0.6, `release` 1 s for a swelling pad; then restore `attack` 0.005 s and `sustain` 0 to continue the pluck lesson. The contrast is time and shape, not a new oscillator.

steps.title: A slider thumb is a jack
steps.text: [Set the `wave` to square](req:osc-wave) (pulse width only matters for a square). Then [Alt-drag the thumb of the **Oscillator**’s `pw` slider onto the **ADSR**’s `env` jack](req:adsr-env-osc-pw) (or drag from `env` and drop it on the thumb). The envelope now also sweeps the pulse width.
steps.why: Dropping a signal on a thumb makes it modulate that parameter, with its own depth in the slider’s ⋮ menu. The same envelope shapes two things at once: loudness and timbre.

steps.title: Undo and redo
steps.text: [Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac), or Commands → Undo](req:undos): the route is gone. [Press Shift+Ctrl+Z (Commands → Redo) and it is back](req:redos,adsr-env-osc-pw). Forty steps of history are kept, cables and modules included.

chapters.title: Subtractive voice
chapters.intro: *Subtractive synthesis* starts with a bright wave and takes harmonics away with a filter. The *cutoff* says where the filter starts cutting, the *resonance* adds a peak there. Moving the cutoff with an envelope, an LFO or a knob is where most of the classic synth sounds come from.
chapters.payoff: Your filter can move by itself and follow a performance knob.
chapters.challenge: Find the moment where a gentle wah becomes a rhythm.

steps.title: Add a Multimode filter
steps.text: [Add a **Multimode**](req:add-filter) and put it between the **Oscillator** and the **VCA**: [**Oscillator** `out` → **Multimode** `in`](req:osc-out-filter-in), [**Multimode** `lp24` → **VCA** `in`](req:filter-lp24-vca-in), and [remove the cable from the **Oscillator** to the **VCA**](req:unplug-osc-out-vca-in).
steps.why: VCO → VCF → VCA is the classic subtractive chain. `lp24` is a 24 dB low pass: steep. `lp12` is gentler, `hp` lets the highs through instead.

steps.title: Sweep the cutoff
steps.text: Play notes on the keys as you [drag `cutoff` down from 16 kHz to about 400 Hz](req:filter-cutoff): the tone gets darker. Move slowly and hear the upper harmonics disappear. Leave `cutoff` below 800 Hz.
steps.why: The `cutoff` slider is logarithmic, like pitch: every octave gets the same distance. Resonance feeds a little of the output back, which makes the filter ring at its cutoff.

steps.title: Give the cutoff a voice
steps.text: Keep playing notes and [raise **Multimode** `res` to about 0.6](req:filter-res). A whistle appears at the cutoff. Optional: sweep `cutoff` to hear the peak travel, then return it below 800 Hz before continuing.

steps.title: Track the keyboard
steps.text: [Tick `track`.](req:filter-track) The cutoff now follows the note, one octave per octave, so high notes stay as bright as low ones. Play up and down.

steps.title: Add an LFO
steps.text: [Add an **LFO**](req:add-lfo) (*low frequency oscillator*). It is an oscillator too slow to hear, made to move other things. [Set its `rate` to about 0.5 Hz.](req:lfo-rate)

steps.title: Wobble the cutoff
steps.text: [Drag the **LFO**’s `out` to the **Multimode**’s `cv` jack.](req:lfo-out-filter-cv) The grey route shows `cv` is built into `cutoff`; `cvamt` sets how far it reaches: [set it to 2 oct](req:filter-cvamt). Hold a note.
steps.why: The `cv` input is additive in octaves: a signal of 1 moves the cutoff up by `cvamt` octaves. A cable dropped on a thumb works differently: it adds to that parameter, with the depth set in the slider’s ⋮ menu.

steps.title: From a slow wah to a wobble
steps.text: Play a run of notes on the keys. Optional: try **LFO** `rate` 0.5 Hz, then 4 Hz. The same cutoff movement becomes a rhythm. Return to 0.5 Hz before continuing; keep notes short if the high resonance is sharp.

steps.title: The knobs follow your click
steps.text: Click any row of the **Multimode**: **Main**’s knobs `K1` to `K4`, on the panel above the keyboard, now turn its first four rows. Dotted lines run from each knob to its row, and a numbered badge marks the row. [Turn **Main**’s `K1`](req:filter-cutoff-turned): the cutoff moves with it.
steps.why: The FM-1 does the same: SELECT picks a device, ALGO a page of four rows, and K1 to K4 turn them. A device is anything at the top of the canvas: a module, or a whole assembly with the rows its card shows.

steps.title: One control, two parameters
steps.text: [Add a **Macro** module](req:macro-added) (+ Module → Macro: one value, one output). [Drag its `out` to the **Multimode**’s `cutoff` thumb](req:main-k1-filter-cutoff), [then drop it on the `resonance` thumb as well](req:main-k1-filter-res): one control can turn several parameters.
steps.why: A module takes up to two different modulation sources, and one source can reach as many of its parameters as you like. A Macro is how a patch gets a performance control: put its `value` on a card, and it lands on a knob like any other row.

steps.title: Set the depth
steps.text: In the ⋮ menu of `cutoff`, [drag the depth of the **Macro** to about 0.5](req:filter-cutoff-depth): it now reaches half as far. Resonance moves with it, since one source on a module shares one depth (*Separate depth* in the menu splits them). A negative value turns it around.

steps.title: Live value and base value
steps.text: Hold a note and watch the `cutoff` slider: the thumb follows the live, wobbling value and a tick marks the base. [Now turn the **Macro**’s `value`](req:main-k1): cutoff and resonance move together, and so does the sound.

chapters.title: Your first assembly
chapters.intro: An *assembly* packs modules into one card that shows only the ports and knobs you choose. It can be saved to your library, reused in other patches, and put inside other assemblies. The five modules you built are about to become one instrument.
chapters.payoff: Five modules fold into your first reusable instrument.
chapters.challenge: Give the instrument a stage name and keep a personal variation.

steps.title: Select the modules
steps.text: [Shift-click the **Oscillator**, **Multimode**, **ADSR**, **VCA** and **LFO**, or drag a box around them on the empty canvas.](req:selected) Selected cards get a highlight. **Main** and **Output** stay outside.

steps.title: Group them
steps.text: [Press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G on a Mac), or Commands → Make assembly, and name it My voice.](req:my-voice-exists) The five cards fold into one that shows the ports which had cables from outside: `pitch`, `gate` and `out`.
steps.why: Grouping changes nothing in the sound. Ports with outside cables are exposed automatically; the rest is hidden until you expose it.

steps.title: Open it up
steps.text: [Click ▸ before the My voice card’s name.](req:my-voice-open) A frame shows the modules inside. Its **card** button chooses what the collapsed card shows.

steps.title: Put two knobs on the card
steps.text: Click **card** on the frame, then click [the **Multimode**’s `cutoff`](req:my-voice-promoted-filter-cutoff) and [the **ADSR**’s `r`](req:my-voice-promoted-adsr-r): they become sliders on the collapsed card. [Click the **LFO**’s `out` too](req:my-voice-exposed-lfo-out): an extra output. Click **done** when you have them (Cmd / Ctrl-click does the same without the button).

steps.title: Resize the frame
steps.text: [Drag the ◢ corner of the frame to give the cards room](req:my-voice-resized) (the arrow keys work on it too). Cards can be moved inside the frame; dragging one out takes it out of the assembly.

steps.title: Close it
steps.text: [Click ▾ at the left of the frame’s header.](req:my-voice-collapsed) One card: `pitch`, `gate`, `out`, the **LFO**’s `out`, `cutoff` and `r`. Play it.

steps.title: Five modules, one instrument
steps.text: Play your new instrument. Move the exposed `cutoff` and release sliders: one changes color, the other changes the tail. Optional: give the card a personal name, then use My voice for the library save so later chapters can find it.

steps.title: Save it to your library
steps.text: [Open the card’s ⋯ menu, choose Save to library and keep the name My voice.](req:my-voice-saved) It is now in + Assembly, under Your library, ready for any patch. LIBRARY → Assemblies is where you rename, export or delete it.

steps.title: Fit the patch to the screen
steps.text: [Commands → Fit patch to screen](req:zooms) scales the canvas so everything is in view. Ctrl+wheel (pinch on touch) zooms freely; Reset canvas scale goes back to 100 %.

chapters.title: An effect assembly
chapters.intro: An *effect* is a module with audio in and audio out. Delay repeats, reverb smears the repeats into a room, chorus thickens with detuned copies. Each has a `mix` slider: dry signal against wet. Chained, they become one effect you can save and reuse.
chapters.payoff: Your instrument carries a room, echoes and stereo movement.
chapters.challenge: Make a small room and an impossible cavern. Compare each with bypass.

steps.title: Hear one echo
steps.text: [Add **Delay**](req:add-delay). Cable [My voice `out` → **Delay** `in`](req:my-voice-out-out-delay-in) and [**Delay** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:delay-out-output-l). [Remove My voice `out` → **Output** `l`](req:unplug-my-voice-out-out-output-l). Tap Note, then Release notes: the repeats continue after the note. Try `mix` at 0, then 0.4.

steps.title: Put the echoes in a room
steps.text: [Add **Reverb**](req:add-reverb). Cable [**Delay** `out` → **Reverb** `in`](req:delay-out-reverb-in) and [**Reverb** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:reverb-out-output-l); [remove **Delay** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:unplug-delay-out-output-l). Compare `size` 0.2 and 0.8: a small room versus a long wash. These are optional listening settings.

steps.title: Spread the sound
steps.text: [Add **Chorus**](req:add-chorus). Cable [**Reverb** `out` → **Chorus** `in`](req:reverb-out-chorus-in), [**Chorus** `l` → **Output** `l`](req:chorus-l-output-l) and [**Chorus** `r` → **Output** `r`](req:chorus-r-output-r); [remove **Reverb** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:unplug-reverb-out-output-l). Play a few notes and compare **Chorus** `mix` 0 and 0.5: the sound widens. Leave the `mix` you like.

steps.title: Tune the space
steps.text: [Set the **Delay**’s `time` to about 375 ms](req:delay-time) and [`fb` (feedback) to 0.5](req:delay-fb), and [the **Reverb**’s `size` to 0.7](req:reverb-size). Play a short note and listen to the tail.
steps.why: *Feedback* sends the delayed signal back into the line: each repeat is quieter than the last. Above 0.9 the repeats barely fade.

steps.title: Hear it with and without
steps.text: Click the **Reverb** card to select it and press B (or click ⏻ in its header): the module is *bypassed* and passes its input straight through. [Press B again to switch it back on](req:bypasses-reverb,bypassed-reverb-off).

steps.title: Group the three
steps.text: [Select the **Delay**, **Reverb** and **Chorus** and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G)](req:my-space-exists). Name the assembly My space. Its card shows `in`, `l` and `r`.

steps.title: Choose its knobs
steps.text: Expand My space, click **card**, then [click the **Delay**’s `time` and `mix`](req:my-space-promoted-delay-time,my-space-promoted-delay-mix) and [the **Reverb**’s `mix`](req:my-space-promoted-reverb-mix), [then collapse it](req:my-space-collapsed). An effect needs few knobs on the outside.

steps.title: Save My space
steps.text: [Choose Save to library in the My space card’s ⋯ menu.](req:my-space-saved) Your library now holds an instrument and an effect; the next chapters use both.

chapters.title: Second instrument: FM
chapters.intro: In *frequency modulation* one oscillator, the *modulator*, wobbles the phase of another, the *carrier*, thousands of times a second. The wobble creates new harmonics: the ratio of the two pitches sets which ones, the depth sets how many. An envelope on the depth makes the classic bright-then-mellow electric piano.
chapters.payoff: Two pure tones became a playable FM instrument with its own space.
chapters.challenge: Save a mellow key and a metallic bell from the same two oscillators.

steps.title: An oscillator, cabled to the pitch
steps.text: [Add an **Oscillator**](req:add-osc) and [cable **Main** `pitch` → **Oscillator** `pitch`](req:main-pitch-osc-pitch). Leave the `wave` on sine: FM wants pure tones.

steps.title: Hear the carrier first
steps.text: [Add a **VCA**](req:add-vca). Cable [the **Oscillator** `out` → **VCA** `in`](req:osc-out-vca-in), [**Main** `gate` → **VCA** `cv`](req:main-gate-vca-cv), and [**VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:vca-out-output-l). Play Note: a pure sine. Stop it before adding the second oscillator.

steps.title: Duplicate it
steps.text: Click the **Oscillator** to select it and [press Ctrl+D (Cmd+D), or Commands → Duplicate selection](req:add-osc-2). The copy keeps its settings. Cables from outside the selection are not copied: [connect **Main** `pitch` to the new **Oscillator**’s `pitch`](req:main-pitch-osc-pitch).

steps.title: Modulator into carrier
steps.text: [Cable the second **Oscillator**’s `out` into the first one’s `pm` input](req:fm-carrier), and [set the first one’s `pm` slider (the depth) to about 2](req:carrier-pm). The first is now the carrier, the second the modulator.
steps.why: `pm` is *phase modulation*, what the DX7 and this oscillator do; it sounds like FM. The depth slider is the *modulation index*: 0 is a sine, 8 is a wall of harmonics.

steps.title: Set the ratio
steps.text: [Set the modulator’s `coarse` to +12](req:modulator-coarse): an octave above the carrier, a 2:1 ratio, hollow like a clarinet. Try +19 (3:1) and +7 for a bell-like clang.
steps.why: Whole-number ratios give harmonic spectra; odd ratios like 1.41 give inharmonic, metallic ones. `coarse` is in semitones.

steps.title: Three colors from two sines
steps.text: Press Note to hold a C4. Optional: compare modulator `coarse` +12 with `pm` 1 (hollow), `coarse` +7 with `pm` 4 (metallic), then `coarse` +12 with `pm` 0.3 (mellow). Return `pm` to 2 and `coarse` to +12 before continuing. Save your favorite as a named variation.

steps.title: Loudness from a level / rate envelope
steps.text: [Add an **Env L/R**](req:add-env). [Remove **Main** `gate` → **VCA** `cv`](req:unplug-main-gate-vca-cv). Cable [carrier `out` → **VCA** `in`](req:carrier-out-vca-in), [**Main** `gate` → **Env** `gate`](req:main-gate-env-gate), [**Env** `env` → **VCA** `cv`](req:env-env-vca-cv), [**VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:vca-out-output-l).
steps.why: **Env L/R** is the DX7 envelope: four levels and the rate to reach each one. The last level, `l4`, is where the note ends after the key is released.

steps.title: Brightness from the same envelope
steps.text: [Alt-drag the carrier’s `pm` thumb onto the **Env**’s `env` jack](req:env-env-carrier-pm). [Set the **Env**’s `l2` and `l3` to 0.3](req:env-l2,env-l3) and [`r2` to 0.4 s](req:env-r2): the note starts bright and mellows while it decays.

steps.title: Group it as FM keys
steps.text: [Select both **Oscillators**, the **Env** and the **VCA** and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G)](req:fm-keys-exists). Name it FM keys. It exposes `pitch` (twice, one per oscillator), `gate` and `out`.

steps.title: Insert My space
steps.text: [Click + Assembly and pick My space under Your library](req:my-space-exists) (the one you saved in chapter 5). It arrives as one card.

steps.title: Put the effect behind the keys
steps.text: Cable [FM keys `out` → My space `in`](req:fm-out-out-space-in-in), [My space `l` → **Output** `l`](req:space-out-l-output-l) and [My space `r` → **Output** `r`](req:space-out-r-output-r). [Remove the cable from FM keys to **Output**](req:unplug-fm-out-out-output-l).

steps.title: Nest the effect inside the instrument
steps.text: Expand FM keys and [drag the My space card into its frame by its header](req:fm-keys-contains-my-space): it becomes part of FM keys, which now exposes `l` and `r` itself. [Collapse FM keys](req:fm-keys-collapsed).
steps.why: Assemblies nest three levels deep. An instrument that carries its own effect is one card wherever you use it.

steps.title: Save FM keys
steps.text: [Choose Save to library in the FM keys card’s ⋯ menu.](req:fm-keys-saved) My space travels inside it.

chapters.title: Plucked and struck
chapters.intro: *Physical models* start from how real instruments work: a burst of energy goes into something that resonates. **String** is a Karplus-Strong string, a short delay line fed back on itself. **Resonator** is a set of tuned resonances like a bar or a bell. **Comb filter** is a resonator you can excite with anything, even noise.
chapters.payoff: You built a string, a resonating body and a breathy pipe.
chapters.challenge: Write a three-note call and answer with muted and ringing settings.

steps.title: A string
steps.text: [Add a **String**](req:add-string). Cable [**Main** `pitch` → **String** `pitch`](req:main-pitch-string-pitch), [**Main** `gate` → **String** `gate`](req:main-gate-string-gate) and [**String** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:string-out-output-l). Each key plucks it.

steps.title: Let it ring
steps.text: [Set the **String**’s `decay` to about 4 s](req:string-decay) and [`damp` to 0.1](req:string-damp): a long, bright note. Optional: switch `burst` to pulse for a harder pick.
steps.why: The string is a delay line as long as one period, with feedback. `decay` sets how much is fed back, `damp` how fast the highs are lost on each round trip.

steps.title: Strike a body with it
steps.text: [Add a **Resonator**](req:add-modal). Cable [**String** `out` → **Resonator** `in`](req:string-out-modal-in) and [**Resonator** `out` → **Output** `r`](req:modal-out-output-r). [Set `struct` to 0.5](req:modal-struct) and [`decay` to 2 s](req:modal-decay): the string now rings a bell-like body.

steps.title: Muted string, ringing body
steps.text: Play a few notes. Optional: try **String** `damp` 0.8 for a muted pick, then 0.1 for a ringing string. Bypass **Resonator** to hear the dry string on the left; turn it back on to hear the body on the right. Return `damp` to 0.1 before continuing.

steps.title: Blow noise through a comb
steps.text: [Add **Noise**, a **Comb filter** and a **VCA**](req:add-noise,add-comb,add-vca). Cable [**Noise** `out` → **Comb filter** `in`](req:noise-out-comb-in), [**Main** `pitch` → **Comb filter** `pitch`](req:main-pitch-comb-pitch), [**Comb filter** `out` → **VCA** `in`](req:comb-out-vca-in), [**Main** `gate` → **VCA** `cv`](req:main-gate-vca-cv), [**VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:vca-out-output-l).
steps.why: A *comb filter* is a tuned delay line: noise through it rings at the note, like breath through a pipe. The **VCA** is a simple on / off here, straight from the `gate`.

steps.title: Make it ring
steps.text: [Set the **Comb filter**’s `fb` to 0.95](req:comb-fb) and [`damp` to 0.1](req:comb-damp): the noise turns into a breathy, whistling tone at the note.

steps.title: Separate the breath from the string
steps.text: Optional: bypass **String** and **Resonator**, then play Note to hear only noise through **Comb filter**. Change **Comb filter** `damp` from 0.1 to 0.8: the breath loses its whistle. Switch both models back on and return `damp` to 0.1 when finished.

steps.title: Slide between notes
steps.text: [Add a **Slew limiter**](req:add-glide). Cable [**Main** `pitch` → **Slew limiter** `in`](req:main-pitch-glide-in) and [**Slew limiter** `out` → **Comb filter** `pitch`](req:glide-out-comb-pitch), and [remove the cable from **Main**’s `pitch` to the **Comb filter**](req:unplug-main-pitch-comb-pitch). [Set `time` to 0.3 s](req:glide-time) and play two notes.
steps.why: **Slew limiter** (*portamento*) slews a control signal: the pitch takes time to arrive. It works on any control cable, not only pitch.

steps.title: Group the pluck
steps.text: [Select the **String** and the **Resonator** and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G)](req:pluck-exists). Name it Pluck. Expand it, click **card**, then [click the **String**’s `decay`](req:pluck-promoted-string-decay) and [the **Resonator**’s `struct`](req:pluck-promoted-modal-struct), and [collapse it again](req:pluck-collapsed).

steps.title: Save Pluck
steps.text: [Choose Save to library in the Pluck card’s ⋯ menu.](req:pluck-saved) Chapter 10 plays it from a melody machine.

steps.title: Play chords
steps.text: [Press **poly** on the Pluck card’s header.](req:poly-parts) Pluck becomes a *poly assembly*, a rack of voice cards: a **Voicing** module appears inside and takes over its `pitch` and `gate` cables, **Main**’s `keys` go into it, and the card shows ×4. Hold a chord: four strings, each with its own note.
steps.why: The **Voicing** does what the processor of a polysynth does: it hands each key you hold to a voice, and a poly assembly runs everything inside it once per voice. Everything outside, the breathy **Comb filter** here, runs once, plays **Main**’s one note and hears the sum of the voices. The Pluck you saved stays a plain assembly: poly is a setting of this copy.

chapters.title: Wavetables and grains
chapters.intro: A *wavetable* oscillator holds a row of waveforms and sweeps through them: the timbre moves without a filter. A *granular* module chops audio into *grains* a few milliseconds long and scatters them in time and pitch: a cloud out of a note. Halfway through, the pad becomes a poly assembly so a held chord can fill the granular buffer. Both are texture tools; zoom out as the canvas grows.
chapters.payoff: You can turn a vowel into a moving, frozen cloud.
chapters.challenge: Capture a chord and find a texture that sounds nothing like its source.

steps.title: A wavetable oscillator
steps.text: [Add a **Wavetable**](req:add-wavetable) and [cable **Main** `pitch` → **Wavetable** `pitch`](req:main-pitch-wavetable-pitch). [Set `bank` to formant](req:wavetable-bank). Next we give it a gated output, then listen to the vowels.

steps.title: Hear a vowel
steps.text: [Add a **VCA**](req:add-vca). Cable [**Wavetable** `out` → **VCA** `in`](req:wavetable-out-vca-in), [**Main** `gate` → **VCA** `cv`](req:main-gate-vca-cv) and [**VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:vca-out-output-l). Start Note and move **Wavetable** `pos`: the vowel changes. The **VCA** keeps the sound under your control.

steps.title: Sweep the table
steps.text: [Add an **LFO** with `rate` 0.2 Hz](req:add-lfo,lfo-rate). [Alt-drag the **Wavetable**’s `pos` thumb onto the **LFO**’s `out`](req:lfo-out-wavetable-pos) (or drop the **LFO**’s cable on the thumb). The position now sweeps on its own.

steps.title: A slow envelope
steps.text: [Add an **ADSR**](req:add-adsr). [Remove **Main** `gate` → **VCA** `cv`](req:unplug-main-gate-vca-cv). Cable [**Main** `gate` → **ADSR** `gate`](req:main-gate-adsr-gate), [**ADSR** `env` → **VCA** `cv`](req:adsr-env-vca-cv), [**Wavetable** `out` → **VCA** `in`](req:wavetable-out-vca-in). [Set `a` to 1 s](req:adsr-a) and [`r` to 2 s](req:adsr-r): a pad.

steps.title: Play chords
steps.text: Select the **Wavetable**, the **VCA** and the **ADSR** (shift-click each, or drag a box around them) and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G) to make them an assembly. [Press **poly** on its header.](req:poly-parts) A **Voicing** module appears inside and takes over the `pitch` and `gate` cables; the card shows ×4. Hold a chord: four notes, each with its own slow envelope.
steps.why: A poly assembly runs everything inside it once per voice, each voice playing its own note. The **LFO** stays outside: one sweep for every voice, as a polysynth’s front panel reaches every voice card. The **Granular** you add next goes outside too, so it hears the sum of the voices and records the whole chord.

steps.title: Into the cloud
steps.text: [Add a **Granular**](req:add-grain). Cable [**VCA** `out` → **Granular** `in`](req:vca-out-grain-in) and [**Main** `gate` → **Granular** `trig`](req:main-gate-grain-trig). Cable [**Granular** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:grain-out-output-l) and [remove **VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:unplug-vca-out-output-l). [Set `size` to 0.15 s](req:grain-size), [`density` to 40](req:grain-density), [`spray` to 0.5](req:grain-spray) and [`pitch` to +12](req:grain-pitch).
steps.why: The granular module records what comes in and plays tiny windows of it, spread over position, time and pitch. `spray` is how far the grains wander from the position.

steps.title: Keep a moment in a cloud
steps.text: Hold a chord on the keyboard for two seconds to fill the buffer, then switch **Granular** `freeze` on. Let go of the keys: the captured sound remains. Optional: change `pitch` and `spray`, then turn `freeze` off before continuing. Bypass **Granular** to compare the dry pad.

steps.title: Place it in the stereo field
steps.text: [Add a **Pan**](req:add-pan). Cable [**Granular** `out` → **Pan** `in`](req:grain-out-pan-in), [**Pan** `l` → **Output** `l`](req:pan-l-output-l), [**Pan** `r` → **Output** `r`](req:pan-r-output-r). [Remove **Granular** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:unplug-grain-out-output-l). Then [drop the **LFO**’s `out` on the `pan` slider’s thumb](req:lfo-out-pan-pos): `pos` is the **Pan**’s built-in input, so the cable goes there.

steps.title: A phaser on the way out
steps.text: [Add a **Phaser** between the **Granular** and the **Pan**](req:add-phaser): [**Granular** `out` → **Phaser** `in`](req:grain-out-phaser-in), [**Phaser** `out` → **Pan** `in`](req:phaser-out-pan-in), and [remove the cable from the **Granular** to the **Pan**](req:unplug-grain-out-pan-in).

steps.title: Zoom out
steps.text: Nine cards no longer fit. [Hold Ctrl (Cmd) and scroll to zoom, pinch on a touch screen, or use Commands → Fit patch to screen](req:zooms).

steps.title: Watch the cloud
steps.text: [Add a **Scope**](req:add-scope), [cable the **Granular**’s `out` into its `a` input](req:grain-out-scope-a) and [switch its screen to FFT](req:scope-mode) (hover the screen for its buttons). Hold a note: the grains smear the harmonics into a band.

chapters.title: Two instruments, one keyboard
chapters.intro: *Layering* is two instruments on one keyboard. A mixer sums them, the arpeggiator plays held keys as a pattern, a *macro range* gives a knob a useful stretch, and the `morph` slider fades between two settings of the whole patch.
chapters.payoff: Your two instruments play together, and a single slider moves their balance.
chapters.challenge: Find a halfway morph you prefer to either endpoint.

steps.title: Insert My voice
steps.text: [Click + Assembly and pick My voice from Your library](req:my-voice-exists). Cable [**Main** `pitch` → its `pitch`](req:main-pitch-my-voice-osc-pitch) and [**Main** `gate` → its `gate`](req:main-gate-my-voice-adsr-gate).

steps.title: Insert FM keys
steps.text: [Insert FM keys the same way.](req:fm-keys-exists) Its card shows two `pitch` inputs, one per oscillator, and a `gate`.

steps.title: Merge the two pitch inputs
steps.text: Expand FM keys. Next to one of the exposed `pitch` inputs [open merge into… and choose the other `pitch`](req:fm-keys-merged-pitch). One `pitch` jack now feeds both oscillators. [Collapse it.](req:fm-keys-collapsed)
steps.why: A *merged input* sends one cable to several inner inputs. Split undoes it.

steps.title: Cable the second instrument
steps.text: [Cable **Main** `pitch` → FM keys `pitch`](req:main-pitch-fm-keys-osc-pitch) and [**Main** `gate` → FM keys `gate`](req:main-gate-fm-env-gate). Both instruments are ready for the mixer in the next step.

steps.title: Mix them
steps.text: [Add a **Mixer 4**](req:add-mixer). Cable [My voice `out` → `in1`](req:my-voice-out-out-mixer-in1), [FM keys `l` → `in2`](req:space-out-l-mixer-in2), [FM keys `r` → `in3`](req:space-out-r-mixer-in3), and [**Mixer** `out` → **Output** `l` and `r`](req:mixer-out-output-l,mixer-out-output-r). `l1`..`l4` are the levels.

steps.title: Hear what each layer contributes
steps.text: Play a few notes on the keys. Optional: put **Mixer** `l2` and `l3` at 0 to hear My voice alone; restore them, then put `l1` at 0 to hear FM keys alone. Bring `l1` back up until neither layer hides the other. This balance is your choice.

steps.title: Let the arpeggiator play
steps.text: Open **Arpeggiator** on the **Main** panel and [press Space (or Commands → arpeggiator)](req:arp-play). Hold a chord: the keys are played one after another at the rate shown.

steps.title: A control with a range
steps.text: [Cable a **Macro**’s `out` (add one) to My voice’s `cutoff` thumb](req:main-k2-my-voice-cutoff). Open the ⋮ menu of My voice’s `cutoff`, tick *Play between two values*, then [set the ends to 150 Hz and 4000 Hz](req:my-voice-cutoff-range). Leave its depth at 1 so the Macro reaches both ends.
steps.why: A macro range maps the Macro’s whole travel onto a slice of the parameter: the useful part of the `cutoff` instead of 20 Hz to 16 kHz.

steps.title: Keep a variation
steps.text: Press **Save** (in the PATCH panel, or Commands → Save patch): Your patches now keeps this sound as "Tutorial duo". Then change a few sliders, the mixer levels for one. [Change My voice’s `cutoff` too](req:my-voice-cutoff-changed). The saved copy is a *variation*: the next step fades between it and what you hear now.

steps.title: Fade to the variation
steps.text: On **Main**, [open the B side picker and choose the saved "Tutorial duo"](req:morph-target). [Move `morph` from 0 to 1, then leave it halfway](req:main-morph). You now hear a continuous change between the variation and what you changed since.
steps.why: A *morph target* must have the same modules and cables. The saved variation is a complete compatible patch; selecting it copies its parameters into the B side. **Main** itself is not morphed.

chapters.title: A random melody machine
chapters.intro: A *sequencer* is a clock and a value per step. A random one samples noise on every tick; a *quantizer* snaps the values to a scale so they become notes; a pulse turns each tick into a gate of a chosen length. The instruments you saved will play whatever the machine comes up with.
chapters.payoff: Chance and a written sequence now share one musical clock.
chapters.challenge: Write a four-note answer to the random machine.

steps.title: A clock
steps.text: [Add an **LFO**](req:add-lfo), [set its `wave` to square](req:lfo-wave) and [its `rate` to 4 Hz](req:lfo-rate). A square wave is a *clock*: its rising edge is a *tick*.

steps.title: Divide it
steps.text: [Add a **Clock divider**](req:add-clkdiv) and [cable **LFO** `out` → **Clock divider** `clock`](req:lfo-out-clkdiv-clock). Its outputs `out`, `d2`, `d4` and `d8` tick every `div`, 2, 4 and 8 ticks.

steps.title: A random value per tick
steps.text: [Add **Noise**](req:add-noise) and [an **S&H** (*sample and hold*)](req:add-sh). Cable [**Noise** `out` → **S&H** `in`](req:noise-out-sh-in) and [**Clock divider** `out` → **S&H** `clock`](req:clkdiv-out-sh-clock). On every tick the **S&H** grabs the noise’s value and holds it.

steps.title: Snap it to a scale
steps.text: [Add a **Quantizer**](req:add-quant), [cable **S&H** `out` → **Quantizer** `in`](req:sh-out-quant-in) and [set `scale` to pent min](req:quant-scale). Random voltages become notes of a pentatonic minor scale.
steps.why: Pitch is a control signal: one unit per octave, a semitone is a twelfth. The quantizer rounds to the nearest note of the scale, which is why random noise sounds like a melody.

steps.title: Play Pluck with it
steps.text: [Insert Pluck from Your library](req:pluck-exists). Cable [**Quantizer** `out` → Pluck `pitch`](req:quant-out-pluck-string-pitch), [**Clock divider** `out` → Pluck `gate`](req:clkdiv-out-pluck-string-gate) and [Pluck `out` → **Output** `l`](req:pluck-out). The machine plays on its own now.

steps.title: FM keys on every second tick
steps.text: [Add a **Pulse** with `time` 0.05 s](req:add-pulse,pulse-time) and [cable **Clock divider** `d2` → **Pulse** `trig`](req:clkdiv-d2-pulse-trig). [Insert FM keys](req:fm-keys-exists); cable [**Quantizer** `out` → FM keys `pitch`](req:quant-out-fm-keys-osc-pitch), [**Pulse** `out` → FM keys `gate`](req:pulse-out-fm-env-gate), [FM keys `l` → **Output** `r`](req:space-out-l-output-r).
steps.why: A divider passes selected input pulses with their original width. **Pulse** makes a predictable 0.05 s gate regardless of the clock’s pulse width.

steps.title: Let chance write the first phrase
steps.text: Listen for several repeats before replacing the random source. Optional: change **Quantizer** `scale` and hear the same random movement obey another set of notes. Return to pent min; the next step lets you write a four-note reply.

steps.title: A written melody instead
steps.text: [Add a **Sequencer**](req:add-seq), [cable **Clock divider** `out` → **Sequencer** `clock`](req:clkdiv-out-seq-clock) and [**Sequencer** `out` → **Quantizer** `in`](req:seq-out-quant-in), and [remove the cable from the **S&H** to the **Quantizer**](req:unplug-sh-out-quant-in). Set `s1`..`s4` to a few different values; [`len` to 4](req:seq-len).
steps.why: The **Sequencer**’s steps are the same kind of signal the **S&H** made, just chosen by you. Through the quantizer the steps land on scale notes whatever you set them to.

steps.title: Lock to the arpeggiator’s clock
steps.text: [Cable **Main** `clock` → **Clock divider** `clock`](req:main-clock-clkdiv-clock) and [remove the **LFO**’s cable to it](req:unplug-lfo-out-clkdiv-clock); [set the **Clock divider**’s `div` to 6](req:clkdiv-div). [Add a second **Clock divider**](req:add-clkdiv-2): [first `out` → second `clock`](req:clkdiv-out-clkdiv2-clock), [second `d2` → **Pulse** `trig`](req:clkdiv2-d2-pulse-trig); [remove first `d2` → **Pulse** `trig`](req:unplug-clkdiv-d2-pulse-trig). Press Space: **Main**’s `clock` now ticks 24 times per beat at the arp tempo, and on the FM-1 it follows MIDI clock.

steps.title: Hear the machine lock together
steps.text: [Press Space to start the arpeggiator clock.](req:arp-play) Change **Main**’s tempo: the written melody, Pluck and every-second-tick FM part stay together. Optional: change `s1`–`s4` to write a four-note answer to the random melody.

chapters.title: Drums from noise
chapters.intro: Most drum sounds are noise or a short tone with a very fast envelope. A hi-hat is filtered noise that dies in a tenth of a second; a kick is a sine whose pitch drops; a snare is both. You build the hat, borrow the kick and snare from the factory assemblies, and clock them from a divider.
chapters.payoff: Noise became a hat, a kit, and a small performance with your own instruments.
chapters.challenge: Perform eight bars: establish the beat, bring in the melody, add a fill, return home.

steps.title: Noise through a high pass
steps.text: [Add **Noise**](req:add-noise) and [a **Multimode**](req:add-filter). [Cable **Noise** `out` → **Multimode** `in`](req:noise-out-filter-in) and [set the `cutoff` to about 6 kHz](req:filter-cutoff): the **Multimode**’s `hp` output is the hiss of a hat.

steps.title: A very short envelope
steps.text: [Add an **Env L/R**](req:add-env) and [a **VCA**](req:add-vca). Cable [**Multimode** `hp` → **VCA** `in`](req:filter-hp-vca-in), [**Main** `gate` → **Env** `gate`](req:main-gate-env-gate), [**Env** `env` → **VCA** `cv`](req:env-env-vca-cv), [**VCA** `out` → **Output** `l`](req:vca-out-output-l). [Set `l1` to 1](req:env-l1), [`r1` to 0.001 s](req:env-r1), [`l2` to 0](req:env-l2), [`r2` to 0.08 s](req:env-r2), [`l3` to 0](req:env-l3) and [`l4` to 0](req:env-l4). Hold a key: one crisp hiss dies away and stays silent.

steps.title: Group it as Hat and save it
steps.text: [Select the **Noise**, **Multimode**, **Env** and **VCA**, press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G) and name it Hat](req:hat-exists). [Choose Save to library in its ⋮ menu](req:hat-saved).

steps.title: Borrow a kick and a snare
steps.text: Click + Assembly and [insert kick and snare from the Drums shelf](req:kick-exists,snare-exists). Expand one to see how it is built: a kick is a sine with a pitch envelope.

steps.title: A clock and a divider
steps.text: [Add an **LFO** (square, 8 Hz)](req:add-lfo,lfo-wave,lfo-rate) and [a **Clock divider** with `div` 2](req:add-clkdiv,clkdiv-div). [Cable **LFO** `out` → **Clock divider** `clock`](req:lfo-out-clkdiv-clock).

steps.title: A pattern from the divisions
steps.text: Cable [**LFO** `out` → Hat `gate`](req:lfo-out-hat-gate-gate) (every eighth), [**Clock divider** `d2` → kick `gate`](req:drum-triggered-kick-d2) (every beat) and [**Clock divider** `d4` → snare `gate`](req:drum-triggered-snare-d4) (every second beat). [Remove the cable from **Main**’s `gate` to the Hat](req:unplug-main-gate-hat-gate-gate).

steps.title: Mix the kit
steps.text: [Add a **Mixer 4**](req:add-mixer): [kick `out` → `in1`](req:drum-out-kick-in1), [snare `out` → `in2`](req:drum-out-snare-in2), [Hat `out` → `in3`](req:hat-out-out-mixer-in3), and [**Mixer** `out` → **Output** `l` and `r`](req:mixer-out-output-l,mixer-out-output-r). [Remove the Hat’s own cable to **Output**](req:unplug-hat-out-out-output-l). [Set `l1` to 0.9](req:mixer-l1) and [`l3` to 0.4](req:mixer-l3).

steps.title: Place the backbeat
steps.text: [Build the beat below](req:beat): three **Sequencers** replace the divider gates. At 120 bpm, kick lands on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, and hats on each beat. A step at −1 is a rest; 0 is a hit. Optional: change one rest into an extra hit and listen to the push it creates.
steps.why: Each **Sequencer** receives the same 4 Hz clock. Its `gate` triggers one drum. The sequencer advances on the first tick, so the first sounding slot is `s2`; `s1` is the last eighth of the bar.

steps.title: An eight-bar miniature
steps.text: [Build the arrangement below](req:performance). It adds steady eighth-note hats. Bars 1–2 establish your beat; 3–6 add your saved Pluck melody; bar 7 opens the hats for a flourish; bar 8 returns to the beat. It repeats every 16 seconds at 120 bpm. Change the kick **Sequencer**’s hit values to change the melody; expand Eight-bar arrangement to change the form; your patch stores the performance.
steps.why: One divider ticks once per bar. A slow **Sequencer** brings in the melody and lengthens the hat tail for a flourish. The same clock drives the notes and the form. If you skipped Pluck, the bundled instrument stands in for it.

steps.title: Share it
steps.text: [Press Share in the PATCH panel (the arrow beside the save icon) and press Copy link](req:shares): it copies a link to this patch to your clipboard. Anyone who opens it gets the beat, your Pluck instrument and the eight-bar arrangement. Name and save a personal variation at the finish.

chapters.title: Voicing
chapters.intro: How a synth deals with *several keys*: one note or many, whether a new key restarts the envelopes (*legato*), which key wins, how pitch slides between notes (*portamento*), and how one oscillator becomes a thick stack. The voice here is a *poly assembly* fed by a **Voicing** module, the synth’s processor: its settings and outputs decide all of that. At the end it drifts out of spec like an old analog polysynth.
chapters.payoff: Your voice glides only when you play legato, stacks detuned copies and drifts like real hardware.
chapters.challenge: Find the smallest depths for the two **Random** modules that still make a chord sound alive.

steps.title: Mono, legato
steps.text: This voice is a *poly assembly* whose **Voicing** has one voice, so it is **mono**: one note at a time. The allocator’s card holds its settings: `voices`, `assign`, `legato`, `priority` and `unison`; the voice cards’ own flaws are under **voices ▾**, next to the frame’s name. Hold a key, then press a second one without letting go of the first, and release it again. The pitch jumps, but the envelope does not start over: the gate stays up while any key is down. That is **legato**, what `legato` `auto` does with one voice.
steps.why: Every analog monosynth had to decide what a second key does. Most of them (a Minimoog, an SH-101 in its default) simply re-pitch the oscillator: the filter and amplitude envelopes keep going. The **Voicing** takes **Main**’s `keys` and gives the modules around it their `pitch` and `gate`, one pair per voice.

steps.title: Restart on every key
steps.text: [Set the voice’s `legato` to `off`.](req:poly-legato) Now play overlapping keys again: every new key, and every release that falls back to a held key, restarts the envelope (you hear the attack each time).
steps.why: `on` never restarts, not even when a part is taken over for a new note; `auto` is legato with one part and a restart for a taken-over part.

steps.title: Which key wins
steps.text: Hold a low key and keep it down, then play a melody above it. With `last` the newest key always sounds. [Set the voice’s `priority` to `low`](req:poly-priority): the held bass note wins until you let go, then the melody takes over.
steps.why: `high` is the opposite: the top key wins, which makes trills against a held upper note. With several voices, priority only decides which note gives up its voice when you hold more keys than there are voices.

steps.title: Portamento
steps.text: [Add a **Slew limiter**](req:add-glide) and [drag it into the voice’s frame](req:inside-poly-glide): now it belongs to the voice. Put it into the pitch path: [**Voicing** `pitch` → **Slew limiter** `in`](req:part-pitch-glide-in), [**Slew limiter** `out` → **Oscillator** `pitch`](req:glide-out-osc-pitch), and [remove the cable from the allocator’s `pitch` to the **Oscillator**](req:unplug-part-pitch-osc-pitch). Every note now slides from the last one.
steps.why: Gliding on every note, overlapping or not, is what Serum calls *always*. The Slew limiter works on any control signal, not only pitch. Outside the frame it would run once and glide the sum of the voices’ pitches.

steps.title: Glide only when legato
steps.text: [Turn **Slew limiter** `time` all the way down](req:glide-time-short), then [drop the **Voicing**’s `legato` on the `time` thumb](req:part-legato-glide-time) and [set its depth in the `time` ⋮ menu to about 0.6](req:glide-time-depth). Detached notes now jump, overlapping notes slide.
steps.why: The allocator’s `legato` output is high while a voice’s note started over a held one. Added to the glide time, it switches portamento on only when you play legato: the 303 slide, or Serum with *always* off.

steps.title: Longer glides for bigger jumps
steps.text: [Set **Slew limiter** `curve` to `lin`.](req:glide-curve-lin) The glide now moves at a constant speed, so a semitone is quick and an octave takes its time.
steps.why: Serum calls this *scaled*. Another way: the allocator’s `jump` is the voice’s last pitch step in octaves; through a **Math** module’s `abs` into the glide time it does the same with the exponential curve.

steps.title: Unison
steps.text: [Set **Oscillator** `unison` to 3 or more](req:osc-unison) and [`detune` to 15 cents or more](req:osc-detune). The copies drift against each other and the sound widens.
steps.why: Each unison copy is a whole oscillator, detuned between −detune and +detune. The FM-1 allows five per oscillator.

steps.title: Blend and stack
steps.text: [Pull **Oscillator** `blend` below 0.35](req:osc-blend): the centre copy comes forward and the detuned ones fall back. Then [set `stack` to `+oct`](req:osc-stack): every other copy plays an octave higher.
steps.why: `blend` 0 is the centre copy alone, 1 only the detuned ones; the level stays the same either way. The stacks are `+oct`, `+5th`, `+oct+5th` and `-oct`.

steps.title: Several notes
steps.text: [Set the **Voicing**’s `voices` to 4](req:poly-parts) and play a chord. Every note gets its own oscillator, glide, filter and envelope: the cards inside show ×4.
steps.why: `assign` decides which free part a new note takes: `rotate` goes round like the voice cards of an old polysynth, `lowest` always tries the first part, `reuse` gives a key back the part that played it last. Each part glides from the note it played before.

steps.title: Drift
steps.text: Real oscillators never stay exactly in tune. [Add a **Random**](req:add-random), [drag it into the voice’s frame](req:inside-poly-random) and [set its `mode` to walk](req:random-mode). [Drop its `out` on the **Oscillator**’s `fine` thumb](req:random-out-osc-fine) and [set the depth in the `fine` ⋮ menu between 0.03 and 0.2](req:osc-fine-depth). Hold a chord: every part wanders slowly on its own, and none of them sits exactly on pitch.
steps.why: Inside a poly assembly each part has its own copy of the **Random**, with its own value. `fine` spans ±100 cents, so a depth of 0.05 is ±5 cents, like a warmed-up analog synth; 0.3 sounds like one that needs service. `rate` sets how often the walk picks a new target.

steps.title: Tolerances
steps.text: In an analog polysynth every voice is built from slightly different parts. [Add a second **Random**](req:add-random-2), [drag it into the frame too](req:inside-poly-random-2) and leave its `mode` at fixed. [Drop its `out` on the **Multimode** `cutoff` thumb](req:random2-out-filter-cutoff) and [set its depth in the `cutoff` ⋮ menu between 0.05 and 0.3](req:filter-cutoff-depth). Play the same chord: now every note has its own brightness.
steps.why: `fixed` is a value between −1 and 1 that never changes, different in every part, like the tolerances of a real instrument’s voice cards. Patched with a small depth into cutoffs, envelope times or `fine`, it makes the notes differ the way real hardware does.

steps.title: Flaws by hand
steps.text: The Randoms pick their values for you. Each voice card also has flaws you set yourself: open **voices ▾** next to the voice’s name and give every voice its own detune, drift, brightness, envelope time and level. Make one voice a little flat and slow, another bright, and play a chord.
steps.why: The flaws are stored with the patch, so it sounds the same every time it loads, on the FM-1 too.

chapters.title: Overview for advanced users
chapters.intro:
A quick look around for people who already patch: no cable basics, just what is different here. It runs on a finished patch, Warm Pad: two detuned saws through a filter and a VCA, then echo and reverb. Play it from your computer keyboard or a MIDI keyboard whenever you like.

Matryoshka is a modular in the Nord Modular tradition. It runs in the browser, and its patches are made to run on the M-VAVE FM-1 too, the four knobs included.
chapters.payoff: That is the tour. The numbered chapters build all of this from an empty canvas, one idea at a time; the tutorial menu lists them if you want the reasoning behind any of it. Press ? for every keyboard shortcut.
chapters.challenge: Patch the **Wavetable** into the free `in3` of the **Mixer 4** inside stack voice and give it `pitch` from **Main**. Then drop the `out` of the **Macro** that moves the **LFO** on the **Wavetable**’s `pos` thumb as well: one control now moves the LFO and sweeps the table.

steps.title: Modules inside modules
steps.text:
stack voice and echo are *assemblies*: groups of modules that behave as one. A closed assembly shows only the jacks and sliders its author brought out, so stack voice reads like a single voice module and echo like a single effect.

[Expand stack voice with ▸ before its name](req:stack-voice-open). Inside are the oscillators, mixer, filter, envelope and VCA.
steps.why: Assemblies nest, save to your library and insert like a module with + Assembly or the palette. Inside an expanded assembly the frame’s **card** button (or Cmd/Ctrl-click) picks which ports and sliders the closed card shows. Select some cards and press Ctrl/Cmd+G to make your own. The FM-1 never sees assemblies: on the FM-1 the patch is the plain modules underneath.

steps.title: Every slider is a jack
steps.text:
Any slider takes a cable: its thumb is a jack. [Drop the **LFO**’s `out` on the thumb of the **Multimode**’s `res` slider](req:lfo-out-filter-res): drag from `out` and let go over the thumb, or Alt-drag the thumb to the jack. Hold a key and hear the resonance breathe.

A modulated thumb shows the live value, and a small tick marks the base you set. A row with a numbered badge is on one of **Main**’s knobs: click any row and its page of four goes on `K1` to `K4`.
steps.why: A thumb drop is a real route: the ⋮ menu beside a slider lists what modulates it, sets each source’s depth and can give it a *macro range* (cutoff from 150 Hz to 4 kHz, say). A module takes up to two different sources; it is the same matrix the FM-1 runs, so the route works on the hardware too.

steps.title: The FM-1 on screen
steps.text:
**Main** is the hardware: `pitch`, `gate` and `vel` from the keys. Its knobs `K1` to `K4` turn the four rows of the device page in focus, picked with DEVICE and PAGE (SELECT and ALGO on the FM-1) or by a click on a row. Every top-level module or assembly is a device, and an assembly’s card is its pages: you design the FM-1’s panel by choosing what the cards show.

The panel also holds the arpeggiator and *morph*: pick a patch of the same structure as the **B side** and the `morph` slider, or its input, glides every parameter between the two.

Polyphony works as on a polysynth: **Main**’s `keys` go into a **Voicing** module, which hands each key to a voice, and a *poly assembly* is the rack of voice cards (marked ×N), one copy per voice. Press *poly* on any assembly’s header and it gets an allocator.

steps.title: One box for everything
steps.text:
Ctrl/Cmd+K (or /) opens the *command palette*. It finds modules, assemblies, patches and every action by name, so you rarely need a menu.

[Add a **Wavetable**](req:add-wavetable): open the palette, type `wavetable` and press Enter.
steps.why: The chips under the search field narrow it to modules, assemblies or patches. Press ? for the shortcuts: B bypasses the selection, Ctrl/Cmd+D duplicates it with its cables, Ctrl/Cmd+G groups it into an assembly.

steps.title: Modules worth a detour
steps.text:
Beyond oscillators, filters, envelopes and VCAs:

- **Wavetable** sweeps its tables with `pos`; **Granular** makes clouds from any input.
- **String** (Karplus-Strong) and **Resonator** (six tuned resonators) are plucked and struck physical models; **Comb filter** adds metallic resonance.
- **Ladder** is a 4-pole filter with drive in the loop; **Multimode** morphs from a 24 dB low pass to a high pass.
- **Freq shifter** is a frequency shifter and **Waveshaper** folds in stages; **Bitcrusher**, **Formant filter** and **Phaser** colour the sound, and the **Compressor** takes a `side` input.
- **Oscillator** does FM: a `pm` input and `fb` feedback, oversampled, plus `unison` and `detune`. **Env L/R** is a DX7-style level/rate envelope.
- **Sequencer**, **Clock divider**, **S&H**, **Quantizer**, **Math** and **Logic** build your own sequencers.

The factory assemblies under + Assembly show many of them at work.

steps.title: Hearing and comparing
steps.text:
- A **Scope** module shows whatever you cable into it, as a waveform or a spectrum.
- B bypasses the selected modules; ⏻ bypasses an assembly.
- *Show changes* lists what moved since you loaded or sent the patch.
- *Share patch…* puts the whole patch in a URL and draws its card for a post.

All of them are in the palette.
